claim: Oxygen (O2) and other dissolved gases such as the gasotransmitters H2S, CO, and NO affect cell metabolism and function.
source: Oxygen (O2) and other dissolved gases such as the gasotransmitters H2S, CO, and NO affect cell metabolism and function.
evidence: This is a general statement about the effects of dissolved gases on cells, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The fluidics system can control dissolved gases while simultaneously measuring parameters of electron transport, metabolism, and secretory function.
source: To evaluate effects of dissolved gases on processes in tissue, we developed a fluidics system that controls dissolved gases while simultaneously measuring parameters of electron transport, metabolism, and secretory function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and methods described throughout the manuscript showing measurements of OCR, cytochromes, lactate, pyruvate, and insulin secretion.

claim: The system revealed a previously unrecognized transient spike in O2 consumption rate (OCR) following replenishment of O2.
source: Protocols aimed at emulating hypoxia–reperfusion conditions resolved a previously unrecognized transient spike in O2 consumption rate (OCR) following replenishment of O2, and tissue-specific recovery of OCR following hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4 demonstrating the transient spike in OCR upon reoxygenation.

claim: The system revealed tissue-specific recovery of OCR following hypoxia.
source: Protocols aimed at emulating hypoxia–reperfusion conditions resolved a previously unrecognized transient spike in O2 consumption rate (OCR) following replenishment of O2, and tissue-specific recovery of OCR following hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing islet and retina recovery rates shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: The system revealed both inhibitory and stimulatory effects of H2S on insulin secretion rate from isolated islets.
source: The system revealed both inhibitory and stimulatory effects of H2S on insulin secretion rate from isolated islets.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 demonstrating concentration-dependent effects of H2S on ISR.

claim: In most cells, the majority of ATP is generated by oxidative phosphorylation, driven by a series of redox reactions in which O2 is the ultimate electron acceptor.
source: In most cells, the majority of ATP is generated by oxidative phosphorylation, driven by a series of redox reactions in which O2 is the ultimate electron acceptor.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cellular energy metabolism.

claim: Hypoxia is linked to many diseases including stroke, cancer, and diabetic complications.
source: Hypoxia is linked to many diseases including stroke, cancer, and diabetic complications.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the medical and scientific literature about the role of hypoxia in disease.

claim: Trace gases produced by cells (H2S, NO, and CO) act as signals to regulate cellular and mitochondrial function.
source: In addition to O2, trace gases produced by cells (H2S, NO, and CO) act as signals to regulate cellular and mitochondrial function (Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prabhakar and Semenza, 2012.

claim: During reoxygenation following ischemia-reperfusion injury, a burst of reactive O2 species (ROS) occurs that can damage proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.
source: Ischemia–reperfusion injury is a condition common to many disease states and it is thought that during reoxygenation a burst of reactive O2 species (ROS) occurs that can damage proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (Chouchani et al., 2016; Zweier et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chouchani et al., 2016 and Zweier et al., 1987.

claim: Quantitative methods to measure the real-time effects of dissolved gases on intact tissue are not available.
source: Yet despite the scientific and clinical importance of dissolved gases, quantitative methods to measure the real-time effects of dissolved gases on intact tissue are not available.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the field prior to the development described in the manuscript.

claim: Investigators who have studied trace gases almost exclusively use aqueous based surrogates/donors of gas.
source: Investigators who have studied trace gases and who are characterizing drugs to attain the same benefits (Chen et al., 2020) almost exclusively use aqueous based surrogates/donors of gas.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020 and represents a characterization of the field.

claim: The equivalence of donor drugs to the gases they are supposed to mimic has not been tested.
source: The equivalence of these drugs to the gases they are supposed to mimic has not been tested (Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2020.

claim: The study of dissolved gases is hampered by the volatility of dissolved gases under conditions where the headspace is not supplied with equilibrium levels of the gas.
source: In addition, the study of dissolved gases is hampered by the volatility of dissolved gases under conditions where the headspace is not supplied with equilibrium levels of the gas (DeLeon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DeLeon et al., 2012.

claim: Commercially available hypoxia chambers control steady-state levels of dissolved gas and have been effectively used for hypoxia studies.
source: Commercially available hypoxia chambers (for instance Baker Ruskinn Cell Culture Workstations) control steady-state levels of dissolved gas and have been effectively and most commonly used for hypoxia studies (Jaakkola et al., 2001; Epstein et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jaakkola et al., 2001 and Epstein et al., 2001.

claim: Microfluidics systems have been developed for establishing cell and tissue models where the three-dimensional structure and cell-to-cell interactions of native tissue can be recreated.
source: Microfluidics systems have been developed for establishing cell and tissue models where the three-dimensional structure and cell-to-cell interactions of native tissue can be recreated, which can be used under steady-state gas compositions (Ren et al., 2013; Manafi et al., 2021; Kimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2013; Manafi et al., 2021; and Kimura et al., 2018.

claim: Some investigators have used the Oroboros machine to characterize the effects of O2 levels on metabolic processes.
source: In addition, some investigators have used the Oroboros machine to characterize the effects of O2 levels on metabolic processes (Stepanova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stepanova et al., 2019.

claim: Existing methods are not designed for implementing and assessing real-time effects of rapid changes in dissolved gas concentrations.
source: However, none of these methods are designed for implementing, and assessing real-time effects of, rapid changes in dissolved gas concentrations.
evidence: This is an assertion about the limitations of existing methods based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: The Seahorse flux analyzer measures OCR and extracellular acidification rate on cell monolayers.
source: The Seahorse flux analyzer measures OCR and extracellular acidification rate (mostly from glycolysis and the TCA cycle) on cell monolayers (Wu et al., 2007) and has been extensively utilized across many fields.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2007.

claim: The Seahorse flux analyzer is not designed to maintain tissue in physiological buffers or to control dissolved gas levels.
source: However, it is not designed to maintain tissue in physiological buffers or to control dissolved gas levels.
evidence: This is an assertion about the limitations of the Seahorse system based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: The earlier version of the flow culture system demonstrated the ability to maintain a range of tissues (including islets, retina, liver, and brain) over hours and days.
source: In previous reports, we described an earlier version of our flow culture system and demonstrated its ability to maintain a range of tissues (including islets, retina, liver, and brain) over hours and days (Neal et al., 2016; Neal et al., 2015; Sweet et al., 2009; Gilbert et al., 2008; Weydt et al., 2006; Bisbach et al., 2020) while continuously assessing metabolic and functional effects of test compounds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous publications by the authors.

claim: Permeation tubes are commonly used devices for calibration of safety equipment that detect toxic gases such as CO and H2S.
source: Permeation tubes are commonly used devices for calibration of safety equipment that detect toxic gases such as CO and H2S.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the industrial use of permeation tubes.

claim: Permeation tubes consist of liquified gas housed under pressure in a metal jacket, where the gas continuously leaks through a membrane at a steady and accurately calibrated rate.
source: They consist of liquified gas housed under pressure in a metal jacket, where the gas continuously leaks through a membrane at a steady and accurately calibrated rate.
evidence: This is a description of how permeation tubes work, based on established knowledge.

claim: Under physiological conditions, OCR can increase in response to changes in substrate supply (increased supply of electrons generated from metabolism) and/or demand (as stimulated by ADP).
source: Under physiological conditions, OCR can increase in response to changes in substrate supply (increased supply of electrons generated from metabolism) and/or demand (as stimulated by ADP Chance and Williams, 1956b; Wilson et al., 1979; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chance and Williams, 1956b and Wilson et al., 1979, as well as Figure 1.

claim: Metabolism of fuels is reflected by a proportional change in cytochrome reduction and OCR: as the number of electrons bound to cytochromes increase, OCR increases by mass action.
source: Metabolism of fuels is reflected by a proportional change in cytochrome reduction and OCR: as the number of electrons bound to cytochromes increase, OCR increases by mass action (a 'push' system).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial metabolism.

claim: Increased ATP usage by energy-utilizing cell functions with a corresponding increase in ADP leads to increased OCR, but without increased cytochrome c reduction.
source: In contrast, increased ATP usage by energy-utilizing cell functions (importantly ion flux and biosynthesis) with a corresponding increase in ADP leads to increased OCR, but without increased cytochrome c reduction (a 'pull' system) (Brown, 1992; Sweet and Gilbert, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown, 1992 and Sweet and Gilbert, 2006.

claim: OCR changes mediated by substrate supply vs. ATP usage can be distinguished by measuring OCR and cytochrome reduction concomitantly.
source: In this way, OCR changes mediated by substrate supply vs. ATP usage can be distinguished, and these fingerprints are informative in understanding mechanisms mediating changes in the ETC induced by H2S and O2.
evidence: This is based on logical inference from the principles of mitochondrial metabolism described.

claim: O2 can influence glycolysis (known as the Pasteur effect).
source: In addition to regulating ETC activity, O2 can also influence glycolysis (known as the Pasteur effect Krebs, 1972; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krebs, 1972 and Figure 1.

claim: [lactate]/[pyruvate] ratio is proportional to the cytosolic redox state ([NADH]/[NAD]).
source: Due to the equilibrium status of LDH, [lactate]/[pyruvate] ratio is proportional to the cytosolic redox state ([NADH]/[NAD]) (Williamson et al., 1967), so by measuring both lactate and pyruvate, changes in the rate of lactate production rate due to alterations in glycolytic flux vs. cytosolic redox state can be distinguished.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Williamson et al., 1967.

claim: H2S can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase.
source: H2S can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase (Khan et al., 1990) and it also can donate electrons to cytochrome c (Vitvitsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Khan et al., 1990.

claim: H2S can donate electrons to cytochrome c.
source: H2S can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase (Khan et al., 1990) and it also can donate electrons to cytochrome c (Vitvitsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vitvitsky et al., 2018.

claim: All previous reports have described only inhibition of ISR by H2S.
source: However, with respect to pancreatic islets, all previous reports have described only inhibition of ISR (Ali et al., 2007; Niki and Kaneko, 2006; Wu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2005; Bełtowski et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies: Ali et al., 2007; Niki and Kaneko, 2006; Wu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2005; Bełtowski et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2013.

claim: Secretagogues that affect ISR by isolated islets including glucose, arginine, amino and fatty acids, acetylcholine, GLP-1 as well as sulfonylureas and GLP-1 analogs, also manifest their effects in vivo.
source: Secretogogs that affect ISR by isolated islets including glucose, arginine, amino and fatty acids, acetylcholine, GLP-1 as well as sulfonylureas and GLP-1 analogs, also manifest their effects in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relevance of isolated islet models.

claim: Isolated islets are a validated and highly relevant model.
source: Therefore, isolated islets are a validated and highly relevant model with which to test our flow culture system.
evidence: This is based on inference from the previous statement about the in vivo relevance of isolated islet responses.

claim: OCR by islets increased with increased glucose concentration.
source: As expected, OCR increased with increased glucose concentration, and decreased with lower O2 tension (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OCR by islets decreased with lower O2 tension.
source: As expected, OCR increased with increased glucose concentration, and decreased with lower O2 tension (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a transient spike of OCR when O2 in the media was restored to islets.
source: Notably, there was a transient spike of OCR when O2 in the media was restored.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OCR by islets approached a steady state that was about 55% of the prehypoxic level of OCR after reoxygenation.
source: OCR then approached a steady state that was about 55% of the prehypoxic level of OCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Glucose provided more reducing power to drive cytochrome c to its reduced state in islets.
source: Consistent with these scenarios, glucose provided more reducing power to drive cytochrome c to its reduced state (in parallel with OCR), whereas hypoxia favored the reduced state of cytochrome c by slowing its oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hypoxia favored the reduced state of cytochrome c by slowing its oxidation in islets.
source: Consistent with these scenarios, glucose provided more reducing power to drive cytochrome c to its reduced state (in parallel with OCR), whereas hypoxia favored the reduced state of cytochrome c by slowing its oxidation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following the return to 21% O2, cytochrome c reduction in islets reached a steady state of 42% of the prehypoxic levels.
source: Following the return to 21% O2, cytochrome c reduction reached a steady state of 42% of the prehypoxic levels, consistent with incomplete recovery of OCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stimulation of ISR by glucose in the presence of 21% O2 was suppressed in low O2.
source: Stimulation of ISR by glucose in the presence of 21% O2 was suppressed in low O2, and ISR recovered to 44% of its original level of stimulation after reoxygenation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ISR recovered to 44% of its original level of stimulation after reoxygenation.
source: Stimulation of ISR by glucose in the presence of 21% O2 was suppressed in low O2, and ISR recovered to 44% of its original level of stimulation after reoxygenation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intraislet Ca2+ increased in response to the increase in glucose.
source: As expected, intraislet Ca2+ increased in response to the increase in glucose.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In response to a decrease in O2, Ca2+ fluorescence in islets rose 3-fold, presumably reflecting a loss of energy-dependent pumping of Ca2+ out of the cells.
source: Subsequently, in response to a decrease in O2, Ca2+ fluorescence rose 3-fold, presumably reflecting a loss of energy-dependent pumping of Ca2+ out of the cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Ca2+ in islets recovered fully to prehypoxic levels when O2 was returned to normal levels.
source: In contrast to OCR and ISR parameters, Ca2+ recovered fully to prehypoxic levels when O2 was returned to normal levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Extracellular ratios of lactate and pyruvate reflect intracellular regulation of these two compounds.
source: To track shifts between glycolytic and mitochondrial energy generation in real time, fractions collected from the outflow were assayed for lactate and pyruvate. We predicted that extracellular ratios of these two analytes reflect intracellular regulation of these two compounds.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the experiments with INS-1 cells.

claim: Most of the pyruvate made in islets is transported into mitochondria.
source: INS-1 cells were used instead of islets because most of the pyruvate made in islets is transported into mitochondria (MacDonald, 1990) since they do not have significant capacity for plasma membrane transport of lactate or pyruvate (Ishihara and Wollheim, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacDonald, 1990 and Ishihara and Wollheim, 2000.

claim: Islets do not have significant capacity for plasma membrane transport of lactate or pyruvate.
source: INS-1 cells were used instead of islets because most of the pyruvate made in islets is transported into mitochondria (MacDonald, 1990) since they do not have significant capacity for plasma membrane transport of lactate or pyruvate (Ishihara and Wollheim, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ishihara and Wollheim, 2000.

claim: Oxamate, an inhibitor of LDH, rapidly and completely suppressed lactate release from INS-1 cells.
source: Oxamate, an inhibitor of LDH, rapidly and completely suppressed lactate release from cells (Figure 3A), showing the tight relation between production of lactate from LDH and appearance of lactate in the outflow.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The rate of INS-1 OCR is about 1/4th of islet OCR on a per cell basis.
source: The rate of INS-1 OCR is about 1/4th of islet OCR on a per cell basis, probably reflecting loss of lactate in INS-1 cells that does not occur in islets, in addition to lower rates of synthesis and secretion of insulin.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data from INS-1 cells and islets.

claim: Blocking transport of pyruvate into mitochondria with zaprinast led to a rapid increase in pyruvate release from INS-1 cells.
source: Blocking transport of pyruvate into mitochondria with [zaprinast a blocker of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC; Du et al., 2013)] led to a rapid increase in pyruvate release from cells (Figure 3B) and diminished OCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Du et al., 2013.

claim: Blocking transport of pyruvate into mitochondria with zaprinast diminished OCR in INS-1 cells.
source: Blocking transport of pyruvate into mitochondria with [zaprinast a blocker of the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC; Du et al., 2013)] led to a rapid increase in pyruvate release from cells (Figure 3B) and diminished OCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The rapidity of the changes in lactate and pyruvate production in response to changes in LDH and MPC indicates that membrane transport is fast.
source: Thus, the rapidity of the changes in lactate and pyruvate production in response to changes in LDH and MPC indicates that membrane transport is fast, and at least in this cell line, extracellular lactate and pyruvate will reflect changes in intracellular events controlling lactate and pyruvate with a time delay of no more than a few minutes.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: OCR by retina decreased at low O2.
source: OCR decreased at low O2, and then manifested a transient spike in response to reoxygenation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OCR by retina manifested a transient spike in response to reoxygenation.
source: OCR decreased at low O2, and then manifested a transient spike in response to reoxygenation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OCR by retina approached a steady state of 83% of the prehypoxic rate after reoxygenation.
source: However, in contrast to islets, OCR by retina then approached a much higher recovery (a steady state of 83% of the prehypoxic rate).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Reduced cytochrome c in retina increased to maximal levels during 1% O2 and stayed at this level throughout the 2 hr of low O2.
source: Reduced cytochrome c increased to maximal levels during 1% O2 and stayed at this level throughout the 2 hr of low O2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Upon return of O2 to 21%, cytochrome c reduction in retina recovered to 79% of prehypoxic levels.
source: Consistent with OCR data, upon return of O2 to 21% cytochrome c reduction recovered to 79% of prehypoxic levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Islets did not recover from hypoxia as well as retina.
source: Comparing posthypoxia levels of OCR in retina vs. islets (Figure 5), islets did not recover from hypoxia as well as retina suggesting that the approach can be used to assess sensitivity to the stress of ischemia-reperfusion conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In response to hypoxia, lactate and pyruvate production rates by retina increased, consistent with operation of the Pasteur effect.
source: In response to hypoxia, lactate and pyruvate production rates by retina increased, consistent with operation of the Pasteur effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ratio of lactate/pyruvate in retina increased during low O2 conditions, reflecting the decreased uptake of pyruvate into the mitochondria, and the increase in the cytosolic redox state (NADH/NAD) that occurs during low O2.
source: The ratio of lactate/pyruvate also increased during low O2 conditions (Figure 4B), reflecting the decreased uptake of pyruvate into the mitochondria, and the increase in the cytosolic redox state (NADH/NAD) that occurs during low O2 (Lai and Miller, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to Lai and Miller, 1973.

claim: When H2S was increased until a steady state of 240 μM was reached, ISR from pancreatic islets increased by 35% relative to ISR at 20 mM glucose.
source: When H2S was increased until a steady state of 240 μM was reached, ISR from pancreatic islets increased by 35% relative to ISR at 20 mM glucose (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The increased ISR in response to H2S was sustained for 3 hr.
source: The increased ISR was sustained for 3 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The effect of H2S on ISR was reversible.
source: The effect of H2S was reversible. After purging it from the system, ISR rapidly returned to levels that occurred prior to H2S exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: H2S had no effect on ISR in the presence of 3 mM glucose.
source: In the presence of 3 mM glucose, H2S had no effect on ISR (data not shown), supporting the idea that this reflects a physiologic response of ISR to H2S.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though the data are not shown.

claim: Between 180 and 780 μM H2S, the initial period of stimulation of ISR (peaking between 1 and 1.5 hr after the start of the ramp of H2S) was insensitive to the concentration of H2S.
source: Notably, between 180 and 780 μM H2S (Figure 6B), the initial period of stimulation of ISR (peaking between 1 and 1.5 hr after the start of the ramp of H2S) was insensitive to the concentration of H2S.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect of higher levels of H2S inhibited the ISR rate only between 1.5 and 4 hr following the start of the H2S exposure.
source: In contrast, the effect of higher levels of H2S inhibited the ISR rate only between 1.5 and 4 hr following the start of the H2S exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The initial upslope of ISR in response to H2S occurred with a delay of about 30 min.
source: The initial upslope of ISR occurred with a delay of about 30 min, and both the stimulation and inhibition of ISR were rapidly reversible following the washout of H2S (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both the stimulation and inhibition of ISR by H2S were rapidly reversible following the washout of H2S.
source: The initial upslope of ISR occurred with a delay of about 30 min, and both the stimulation and inhibition of ISR were rapidly reversible following the washout of H2S (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H2S increased intracellular Ca2+ in islets at a concentration that increased ISR.
source: Consistent with a stimulatory effect of H2S on ISR, intracellular Ca2+ increased dramatically upon exposure to H2S, and returned to near pre-H2S levels within a few minutes of washing out the H2S.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ returned to near pre-H2S levels within a few minutes of washing out the H2S.
source: Consistent with a stimulatory effect of H2S on ISR, intracellular Ca2+ increased dramatically upon exposure to H2S, and returned to near pre-H2S levels within a few minutes of washing out the H2S.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Low levels of NaHS had no effect on ISR, and higher concentrations (>1 μM) inhibited ISR.
source: In contrast to dissolved gaseous H2S, low levels of NaHS had no effect, and higher concentrations (>1 μM) inhibited ISR (Appendix 1—figure 1A, B) – consistent with findings of all previous studies that used NaHS as an H2S surrogate (Niki and Kaneko, 2006; Wu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2005; Bełtowski et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2019; Patel and Shah, 2010; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1A, B and citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: NaHS did not increase Ca2+ in islets, and slightly decreased it by amounts that were relatively insensitive to the concentration of NaHS.
source: Similarly, NaHS did not increase Ca2+, and slightly decreased it by amounts that were relatively insensitive to the concentration of NaHS (Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1C.

claim: The H2S generated by NaHS diffuses out of solution and into the gas phase when the media is in contact with a headspace that does not contain gaseous H2S.
source: The likely explanation of the difference between effects of H2S and NaHS is that the H2S generated by NaHS diffuses out of solution and into the gas phase when the media is in contact with a headspace that does not contain gaseous H2S.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A, B.

claim: The H2S in solution emanating from the headspace was higher than that achieved from NaHS.
source: The H2S in solution emanating from the headspace was higher than that achieved from NaHS, but notably it declined when the headspace was purged.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A, B.

claim: H2S from the NaHS had transferred into the headspace.
source: Although the amount in the headspace was close to the detection limit of the H2S measurement method, it was clear from the sharp decline in H2S after unsealing the bottle, that H2S from the NaHS had indeed transferred into the headspace.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2A, B.

claim: Differences in effects of H2S and NaHS occur due to the absence of H2S in solution containing NaHS and HS− is inhibitory for both ISR and Ca2+.
source: Thus, these data support a scenario where differences in effects of H2S and NaHS occur due to the absence of H2S in solution containing NaHS and HS− is inhibitory for both ISR and Ca2+.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data comparing H2S and NaHS effects.

claim: The transient spike of OCR is consistent with a scenario where O2 is the source of oxygen atoms for the ROS.
source: The transient spike of OCR is consistent with a scenario where O2 is the source of oxygen atoms for the ROS.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed transient spike in OCR.

claim: The transient spike of OCR is consistent with the buildup of metabolites such as succinate during ischemia, which could fuel increased oxidation rate.
source: This is also consistent with the buildup of metabolites such as succinate during ischemia (Beach et al., 2020), which could fuel increased oxidation rate.
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Beach et al., 2020.

claim: Gas signaling molecules (CO, NO, and H2S) are generated in most tissues and have wide-ranging effects on function, metabolism, and protection from hypoxia.
source: Gas signaling molecules (CO, NO, and H2S) are generated in most tissues and have wide-ranging effects on function, metabolism, and protection from hypoxia (for reviews Ahmad et al., 2018; Beltowski, 2007; Cheng and Rong, 2017; Krylatov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: The majority of studies on trace gases have utilized aqueous chemical donors such as NaHS instead of H2S.
source: However, due to the difficulty in quantitatively and reproducibly introducing dissolved trace gases into culture media, the majority of studies on these gases have utilized aqueous chemical donors such as NaHS instead of H2S.
evidence: This is a characterization of the field based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: Permeation tubes can introduce trace gases into the carrier gas at exact times and concentrations.
source: Due to the extremely accurate calibration of the rate of release of gases, permeation tubes can introduce trace gases into the carrier gas (the mixture of CO2–O2–N2) present in a gas equilibration system of our perifusion apparatus at exact times and concentrations.
evidence: This is based on the known properties of permeation tubes and the design of the system.

claim: Producers of permeation tubes can provide them with a selection of over 500 gases, including H2S, NO, CO, and ammonia.
source: Producers of permeation tubes can provide them with a selection of over 500 gases, including H2S, NO, CO, and ammonia.
evidence: This is factual information about the availability of permeation tubes.

claim: H2S at concentrations between 140 and 280 μM enhanced glucose-stimulated ISR, which remained elevated for at least 4 hr.
source: Our system bore out this prediction revealing stimulatory effects of H2S on ISR that had not been apparent when exposing islets to a donor of H2S (NaHS). H2S at concentrations (between 140 and 280 μM) enhanced glucose-stimulated ISR, which remained elevated for at least 4 hr.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At higher concentrations of H2S the stimulation of ISR for 90 min still occurs, but at later times ISR was inversely proportional to the H2S ranging from a 35% increase to a 40% decrease.
source: At higher concentrations of H2S the stimulation of ISR for 90 min still occurs, but at later times ISR was inversely proportional to the H2S ranging from a 35% increase to a 40% decrease.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C.

claim: H2S had no effect on ISR at 3 mM glucose, supporting a physiologic mechanism mediating H2S's effect that may be integrated with glucose sensing and secretory response to fuels by the islet.
source: H2S had no effect on ISR at 3 mM glucose, supporting a physiologic mechanism mediating H2S's effect that may be integrated with glucose sensing and secretory response to fuels by the islet (Prentki et al., 2013; Campbell and Newgard, 2021).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and supported by citations to Prentki et al., 2013 and Campbell and Newgard, 2021.

claim: The stimulatory effects of H2S on ISR and Ca2+ directly refute the well accepted conclusions that H2S decreases ISR and Ca2+ by opening KATP channels.
source: The stimulatory effects of H2S on ISR and Ca2+ directly refute the well accepted conclusions that H2S decreases ISR and Ca2+ by opening KATP channels as has been widely reported (Ali et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2019; Shoji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from this study contradicting previous reports cited.

claim: In the absence of H2S in the headspace above the media, dissolved H2S quickly disappears into the headspace.
source: Although it is typically assumed when using NaHS as a source of H2S that NaHS and H2S equilibrate in solution (Olson, 2009), our measurements show that in the absence of H2S in the headspace above the media, dissolved H2S quickly disappears into the headspace, a phenomenon analogous to the behavior of CO2-based buffers.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 2 and a citation to Olson, 2009.

claim: Measurements of effects of NaHS on tissue in open systems such as typical static and perifusion methods contain little H2S.
source: Thus, measurements of effects of NaHS on tissue in open systems such as typical static and perifusion methods contain little H2S.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data showing H2S volatilization.

claim: H2S is generated in islets by the action of three intracellular enzymes.
source: H2S is generated in islets by the action of three intracellular enzymes (Kimura, 2010) but is also a component of blood albeit at levels that are not well established (Whiteman et al., 2010; Karunya et al., 2019; Whitfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kimura, 2010; Whiteman et al., 2010; Karunya et al., 2019; and Whitfield et al., 2008.

claim: H2S is a component of blood albeit at levels that are not well established.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Whiteman et al., 2010; Karunya et al., 2019; and Whitfield et al., 2008.

claim: The range of H2S concentrations that induced changes in ISR are in the range of typical estimates of plasma concentration which range from 30 to 300 μM.
source: It is notable that the range of concentrations that induced changes in ISR, and above which caused inhibition of OCR in liver are in the range of typical estimates of plasma concentration which range from 30 to 300 μM (Olson, 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental results with literature values cited from Olson, 2009.

claim: Intracellular effects of H2S could be mediated by H2S derived from the blood as well as H2S endogenously produced by cells.
source: Therefore, it suggests that intracellular effects of H2S could be mediated by H2S derived from the blood as well as H2S endogenously produced by cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the physiological concentrations observed.

claim: The rate of release of lactate and pyruvate is an integration of the rate of glycolysis less the amount of pyruvate flux into the mitochondria and traversing gluconeogenesis.
source: The rate of release of lactate and pyruvate is an integration of the rate of glycolysis less the amount of pyruvate flux into the mitochondria and traversing gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism.

claim: Both lactate and pyruvate generally increase in response to glycolytic fuels.
source: Thus, both compounds generally increase in response to glycolytic fuels.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of cellular metabolism.

claim: Both lactate and pyruvate rise in cells when O2 is decreased (the Pasteur effect).
source: Importantly for the study of hypoxia, both metabolites rise in cells when O2 is decreased (the Pasteur effect).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the Pasteur effect.

claim: The ratio of cytosolic lactate/pyruvate mirrors the cytosolic NADH/NAD ratio due to the equilibrium status of the LDH reaction.
source: In addition, the ratio of cytosolic lactate/pyruvate mirrors the cytosolic NADH/NAD ratio due to the equilibrium status of the LDH reaction (Newsholme and Start, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newsholme and Start, 1973.

claim: The rapid changes in extracellular lactate and pyruvate support the rapid redistribution between intra- and extracellular compartments.
source: The rapid changes in extracellular lactate and pyruvate support the rapid redistribution between intra- and extracellular compartments, and that real-time measurement of extracellular lactate and pyruvate reflect intracellular events governing intracellular lactate and pyruvate.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

source: The rapid changes in extracellular lactate and pyruvate support the rapid redistribution between intra- and extracellular compartments, and that real-time measurement of extracellular lactate and pyruvate reflect intracellular events governing intracellular lactate and pyruvate.

claim: Retina responded to hypoxia with a classical Pasteur effect: low O2 increased lactate, pyruvate, and lactate/pyruvate ratio.
source: Retina responded to hypoxia with a classical Pasteur effect: low O2 increased lactate, pyruvate, and lactate/pyruvate ratio.

source: Unexpectedly, the loss of energy and ISR following islet exposure to hypoxia were not accompanied by a loss of glucose-stimulated Ca2+, suggesting the mechanism mediating loss of ISR is independent of Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from Figure 2C.

claim: The mechanism mediating loss of ISR during hypoxia is independent of Ca2+ signaling.
source: Unexpectedly, the loss of energy and ISR following islet exposure to hypoxia were not accompanied by a loss of glucose-stimulated Ca2+, suggesting the mechanism mediating loss of ISR is independent of Ca2+ signaling.

claim: Loss of secretory function is more closely associated with bioenergetics than Ca2+.

claim: Flow systems have important advantages over static systems for assessment of cell function.
source: Flow systems have important advantages over static systems for assessment of cell function.
